# What Years of CTV Ad Data Taught Us About Who’s Buying TV


Tim Edmundson | 6 Min Read

Connected TV is a strong performance channel thanks to its targeting and measurement capabilities. These are key elements to any successful performance campaign. But CTV as an ad channel has not always been this way. As innovations and technology developed over the last decade, CTV has gained more budgets and a larger share of marketing strategy. And with that, a place in performance marketers’ media plans.


The data in this piece comes from one performance CTV platform, MNTN’s, which has given us a front row seat to performance marketing’s evolution on CTV. That vantage point has let us witness some interesting trends over time. From the early days of CTV’s perception as an extension of traditional TV media buys, to its wider education and adoption phases (accelerated by consumer habits brought on by the pandemic), one thing is certain: CTV has become a channel that’s accountable for driving measurable outcomes and performance.


Our experience with thousands of advertisers has given us a window into the rise of measurable performance marketing on the TV screen. Granted, marketers who use CTV for performance may be drawn to a platform like ours and may not represent the full spectrum of marketers, including those who focus on pure branding, events, and the like. That’s fair, and something we account for: it’s why we look at the data as a window into examining how performance-minded marketers have embraced CTV. Or rather, Performance TV. So what are some lessons we’ve learned?


# Who’s Buying TV Now


Connected TV hasn’t been something just for existing TV advertisers. There has been a wave of first-time TV advertisers tapping into CTV, due in large part to its ability to function like measurable and targetable digital ad channels. We saw this firsthand; at the start of 2025, over nine in 10 advertisers on the platform were first-time TV advertisers. They’re digital natives by nature, meaning they’ve traditionally found success with channels like paid search and social. Now, however, they’ve taken to Connected TV and brought their digital mindsets with them.

So what does a digital mindset actually look like once it’s on TV? Mostly, it looks like someone refusing to wait. Search and social marketers are used to checking campaigns every morning, shifting budget toward whatever’s converting, running two creatives at once and cutting the loser, and measuring success as they did it. They’ve brought that performance marketing muscle memory with them. None of this is new thinking. It’s just new to the biggest screen they’ve ever bought, and their moving budgets to capitalize on it.


[IAB’s 2026 digital video report](https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/414828/digital-video-ad-spend-to-climb-11-to-82b-iab.html) found that among advertisers increasing CTV spend this year, 54% are moving money from linear TV and 38% are moving it from social media. The budgets arriving on the TV screen are increasingly coming from channels that were always measured.

Using CTV for measurable outcomes has been a growing trend for a while now. Case in point: back in 2022, we saw conversion events increase by 914% year over year across advertiser campaigns run on the platform. The early ‘20s were a time when more advertisers were discovering what sort of objectives they could pursue using the biggest screen in the home. Marketers were eager to do more with TV: measure more, target more, and bring more accountability to their ad spend. The types of goals being measured by advertisers, and the sheer volume of those doing it, were indicative of a sea change under way.


Today, advertisers can measure revenue, return on ad spend, site visits, conversion rates and more. Vital insights once reserved for digital channels have made the jump to the TV screen for advertisers. This, in turn, has made TV an asset for any marketer looking to bring potential customers through the entire funnel.


# How They Use It: A Full-Funnel Approach


Advertisers aren’t just using CTV for top-of-funnel. Rather, many advertisers use it to address the full sales funnel, from top to bottom. Using upper funnel CTV campaigns, advertisers raise awareness, establish touchpoints, and simultaneously generate return on ad spend in the process. Touchpoints like site visits, and outcomes like conversions and associated revenue are attributed to their campaigns.


Similarly, they deploy lower-funnel campaigns such as retargeting. This tactic makes the most of their website traffic (piggybacking off the success of their upper-funnel prospecting campaigns), and re-engages website visitors to bring them back to the site to convert.


An analysis from Digiday and MNTN found that advertisers on the platform who ran upper-funnel prospecting and lower-funnel retargeting campaigns on CTV kept their prospecting live 57% longer than those who didn’t run retargeting.

Source: Digiday/MNTN analysis; MNTN Research,[Data-Driven Insights from 10M+ Hours of CTV Ads](https://research.mountain.com/trends/data-driven-insights-from-10m-hours-of-ctv-ads/) .


And, those who ran both campaigns together generated an average of 34% more return on ad spend (ROAS) than just prospecting alone. More mileage from campaigns and a better return on spend was a benefit we observed across those advertisers. To be clear, these are observations about how one slice of the marketing world behaved rather than a controlled comparison; advertisers who run both are often the ones with bigger budgets and longer planning horizons to begin with.


# What All This Data Adds Up To


So what have we learned about CTV over the years? The fastest-growing group of TV advertisers didn’t come from the world of TV advertising. They came from the digital side of the business, from paid search and social, and they measure TV by site visits, conversions, and return on spend, the same yardsticks they used for those channels. As their share of TV budgets grows, so does the expectation that TV can be held to those numbers. That shift doesn’t belong to any one platform; it’s a change in what advertisers ask of the screen. As we continue to see brands embrace this use case for the ad channel, we’ll keep monitoring what’s going on from where we sit and let you know what we find.
